docs.title: Tekmaturix
docs.text:
Ideas. Innovation. Knowledge.

Tekmaturix is a hub for big ideas — a place to collect breakthroughs in science and mathematics, explore the frontiers of the mind, and turn curiosity into innovations that solve real-world problems.

docs.title: The name
docs.text: Part Symbol Meaning Tek 𒆳 Technology, mastery, advanced knowledge Matu 𒁍 Courage, resilience, never giving up Rix Latin Ruler, leader, innovator

docs.title: The big idea
docs.text:
Most sites document what humanity knows. Tekmaturix also maps what it doesn't — the biggest unsolved problems in science, technology, and society, each with a live status showing where we stand.

Explore the Unsolved →

docs.title: Explore
docs.text:
• Unsolved

    A living map of humanity's biggest open problems — from dark matter to AI alignment — with a progress tracker for each.

  • Innovations

    Ideas that solve real-world problems — a problem → solution library, from first spark to working solution.

  • Knowledge

    Twelve domains — space, oceans, future tech, the brain, ancient civilizations, medicine, and more.

  • Space

    Black holes, exoplanets, JWST discoveries, and the search for life.

  • Oceans

    The frontier below us — 80% unexplored, right here on Earth.

  • Mind & Beyond

    Telepathy, telekinesis, teleportation — what's real, what's not, and the psychology behind it.

docs.title: About
docs.text: Tekmaturix is a hub for ideas, innovations, and knowledge — collecting humanity's breakthroughs and asking what's next.

docs.title: The philosophy
docs.text:
• Tek (𒆳) — master knowledge, don't just consume it
  • Matu (𒁍) — have the courage to explore, question, and keep going
  • Rix — lead by building things that help others

docs.title: What this site believes
docs.text:
1. Big ideas look impossible right before they look obvious.
  2. Curiosity about everything, evidence for anything.
  3. Knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied.
  4. The point of learning is to solve real problems for real people.

docs.title: Innovations
docs.text:
"Innovation is seeing what everybody has seen and thinking what nobody has thought." — Albert Szent-Györgyi

This is where ideas live. Not just technology for its own sake — ideas that make life better, solve problems people actually have, and push what's possible.

docs.title: How an idea becomes an innovation
docs.text:
1. Notice a real problem — something that frustrates people, wastes time, or causes harm
  2. Ask why it hasn't been solved — usually the answer reveals the real challenge
  3. Learn what you need — the knowledge sections of this site exist for exactly this
  4. Build the smallest version that works — courage over perfection (Matu 𒁍)
  5. Share it, get feedback, improve — leadership means shipping (Rix)

docs.title: Innovations that started as "impossible"
docs.text:
Once "impossible" Now everyday Talking to someone across the world instantly Phone calls, video chat Flying machines heavier than air 100,000+ flights per day A library in your pocket Smartphones Machines that understand language AI assistants Seeing inside the human body without cutting MRI, CT scans

The lesson

Every one of these was dismissed by experts of its time. The gap between "impossible" and "obvious" is usually one generation of stubborn innovators.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: • Real-World Problems — the problems worth solving, and my ideas for them

docs.title: Real-World Problems & Solutions
docs.text: A problem → solution library. Every entry names a real problem, the approaches being tried, and where things stand. For humanity's biggest unsolved challenges, see the dedicated Unsolved section.

docs.title: 🌡️ Climate change
docs.text: Problem: rising CO₂ is warming the planet, driving extreme weather and sea-level rise. Solutions in play: renewables (now the cheapest power in history), EVs, carbon removal, fusion, reforestation, grid storage.

docs.title: 💧 Water scarcity
docs.text: Problem: 2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water. Solutions in play: affordable desalination, solar stills, fog harvesting, atmospheric water generators, leak-detection AI, drip irrigation.

docs.title: 🍎 Food waste
docs.text: Problem: ~1/3 of all food produced is wasted, while millions go hungry. Solutions in play: better cold chains, AI demand forecasting, dynamic pricing for near-expiry food, redistribution apps, edible coatings that extend shelf life.

docs.title: 🥤 Plastic pollution
docs.text: Problem: 8M tonnes of plastic enter the ocean yearly; microplastics are everywhere. Solutions in play: river interception, plastic-eating enzymes, compostable bioplastics, deposit-return schemes, redesigning packaging.

docs.title: 🏥 Healthcare access
docs.text: Problem: billions lack affordable, quality healthcare. Solutions in play: telemedicine, AI diagnostics (detecting disease from a phone photo), drone-delivered medicine, low-cost portable devices, community health workers.

docs.title: 🚗 Traffic congestion
docs.text: Problem: cities lose billions of hours and tonnes of emissions to gridlock. Solutions in play: smart traffic lights, congestion pricing, better public transit, remote work, ride-sharing, and eventually autonomous vehicle coordination.

docs.title: 🔋 Energy storage
docs.text: Problem: solar and wind are intermittent — we need to store power for when the sun sets and wind drops. Solutions in play: next-gen batteries, pumped hydro, green hydrogen, gravity storage, thermal storage.

docs.title: 🏠 Affordable housing
docs.text: Problem: housing costs outpace incomes in most cities. Solutions in play: modular & 3D-printed homes, zoning reform, mass timber, prefab construction.

docs.title: My idea log
docs.text:
How to use this

Every time an idea strikes — write it here immediately, even if it seems silly. Review monthly. The habit of capturing ideas matters more than the quality of any single one.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
"The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existing." — Albert Einstein

Innovation runs on knowledge. This section collects the breakthroughs, mysteries, and big questions across every field that fascinates me.

docs.title: The domains
docs.text:
• Space — black holes, exoplanets, JWST, alien-life possibilities
  • Oceans & Deep Sea — deep-sea creatures, mysteries, marine tech
  • Future Technology — AI, robotics, quantum, fusion, BCIs, nanotech
  • Mind & Beyond — telepathy, telekinesis, teleportation, psychology
  • Brain & Psychology — memory, habits, biases, creativity
  • Maths & Science — relativity, quantum, fractals, DNA
  • Philosophy & Philanthropy — thinking well, doing good
  • Ancient Civilizations — lost cities, ancient engineering, mysteries
  • Inventions — the ideas that transformed society
  • Engineering Wonders — bridges, skyscrapers, spacecraft, megaprojects
  • Natural Wonders — volcanoes, mountains, caves, weather
  • Medical Science — the human body, genetics, breakthroughs

Knowledge → Unsolved

Each domain here has a frontier. When you hit the edge of what's known, the Unsolved section picks up — a living map of what humanity is still trying to figure out.

docs.title: Ancient Civilizations & History
docs.text: The past is stranger and more advanced than we usually imagine.

docs.title: Ancient engineering that still baffles us
The Great Pyramid of Giza
docs.text: Built ~2,560 BCE from 2.3 million blocks averaging 2.5 tonnes each, aligned to true north within a fraction of a degree. It was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years. Exactly how it was built is still debated.

docs.title: Roman concrete
docs.text: Roman harbor concrete has survived 2,000 years in seawater — and gets stronger over time. Modern concrete crumbles in decades. Scientists only recently (2023) worked out the self-healing chemistry: "hot mixing" with lime.

docs.title: The Antikythera mechanism
docs.text: A bronze geared "computer" from ~100 BCE, recovered from a Greek shipwreck, that predicted eclipses and planetary positions. Nothing of comparable complexity appears again for 1,400 years.

docs.title: Lost cities & mysteries
docs.text:
• Göbekli Tepe (Turkey) — monumental stone temples built ~11,000 years ago, before agriculture, pottery, or the wheel. It rewrote the timeline of civilization.
  • The Indus Valley — cities like Mohenjo-daro had grid streets and plumbing 4,500 years ago; their writing is still undeciphered.
  • Ancient Amazon — LiDAR is revealing vast lost cities under the rainforest canopy, overturning the myth of an "untouched" Amazon.

docs.title: Historical mysteries still open
docs.text:
• What caused the Bronze Age Collapse (~1200 BCE) — multiple civilizations fell at once?
  • Who were the Sea Peoples?
  • How were the Nazca Lines designed to be seen only from the sky?

Quote

Every "primitive" civilization turns out to be cleverer than we assumed. Humility about the past is good training for humility about the future.

docs.title: Engineering Wonders
docs.text: What humanity can build when ambition meets mathematics.

docs.title: Bridges
docs.text: The Golden Gate (above) was called impossible before it opened in 1937. Today the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge in Japan spans ~2 km in a single leap and is built to survive magnitude-8 earthquakes and typhoon winds.

docs.title: Skyscrapers
docs.text: The Burj Khalifa rises 828 m — half a mile — into the sky. Its buttressed core and tapering shape let it defy wind that would topple a simpler tower. The next generation (Jeddah Tower) aims for 1 km.

docs.title: Aircraft
docs.text: The jet engine turned the planet into a place you can cross in hours. A modern airliner holds ~4 million parts and flies 900 km/h, 12 km up, safely, thousands of times a day.

docs.title: Spacecraft
docs.text: The Saturn V remains the most powerful machine ever flown — 3,000 tonnes, 7.5 million pounds of thrust, to send humans to the Moon with less computing power than a modern calculator. Today Starship is the largest rocket ever built.

docs.title: Dams
docs.text: The Three Gorges Dam generates as much power as ~20 nuclear reactors. The Hoover Dam still holds back the Colorado River after nearly a century.

docs.title: Bullet trains
docs.text: Japan's Shinkansen has carried billions of passengers since 1964 with a near-perfect safety record and average delays measured in seconds. Maglev prototypes exceed 600 km/h.

docs.title: Tunnels
docs.text: The Gotthard Base Tunnel runs 57 km straight through the Alps. The Channel Tunnel links Britain and France beneath the sea.

docs.title: Megaprojects
docs.text:
The International Space Station — a 420-tonne laboratory assembled in orbit from modules built by 15 nations, continuously inhabited since 2000.

Quote

Every wonder here was "too big," "too expensive," or "too dangerous" — until the engineering caught up with the ambition. The next wonders are in Unsolved: Engineering.

docs.title: Future Technology
docs.text: The tools that will define the next 50 years — some already in labs, some just leaving them.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text: Machines that learn, reason, and create. From language models to scientific discovery (AlphaFold solved protein structures biologists chased for 50 years). The open questions — alignment, consciousness, AGI — live in Unsolved: AI.

docs.title: Robotics
docs.text: General-purpose humanoid robots are leaving research labs (Figure, Tesla Optimus, Boston Dynamics). The hard part was never the body — it's the brain: robots that handle the messy, unpredictable real world.

docs.title: Quantum computing
docs.text: Computers that use quantum superposition to solve problems classical machines never could — drug design, materials, cryptography. Still fragile and error-prone. See Unsolved: Computing.

docs.title: Fusion energy
docs.text: The power source of the stars, on Earth. 2022 brought the first net-energy-gain reaction. Limitless clean power if we can make it continuous and cheap — Unsolved: Earth.

docs.title: Brain-computer interfaces
docs.text: Chips that let the mind control machines directly — already restoring movement and speech to paralyzed people (Neuralink, Synchron). The engineered version of "telepathy." See Mind & Beyond.

docs.title: Nanotechnology
docs.text: Building at the scale of atoms — targeted drug delivery that hunts cancer cells, self-cleaning surfaces, ultra-strong materials, and someday molecular machines.

docs.title: Future transportation
docs.text: Reusable rockets, electric aviation, hyperloop, autonomous vehicles, and eVTOL "flying taxis" moving from prototype to pilot programs.

docs.title: Smart cities
docs.text:
Cities that sense and respond — optimizing traffic, energy, water, and waste in real time. The promise is efficiency; the tension is privacy and surveillance.

Where the frontier meets the wall

For each technology above, the exciting part is what it can't do yet — that's exactly what the Unsolved section tracks.

docs.title: Inventions That Changed the World
docs.text: A handful of ideas reshaped everything that came after them.

docs.title: The printing press (1440)
docs.text: Gutenberg's movable type made knowledge copyable and cheap. Literacy, science, the Reformation, and the modern world all trace back to it. Arguably the most important information technology before the internet.

docs.title: Electricity (19th century)
docs.text: Not one invention but a cascade — the battery, the generator, the light bulb, the motor. It turned night into day and powered every machine since.

docs.title: The steam engine (1712 / 1769)
docs.text: The muscle of the Industrial Revolution. For the first time, humanity had power that didn't come from muscle, wind, or water — and could put it anywhere.

docs.title: Vaccines (1796)
docs.text: From Jenner's smallpox vaccine to mRNA, vaccines are the single greatest life-saver in medical history — smallpox, which killed 300 million in the 20th century alone, is eradicated.

docs.title: The computer (20th century)
docs.text: From room-sized machines to the chip in your pocket. Computing didn't just automate work — it created entirely new worlds of software, data, and AI.

docs.title: The internet (1969 → 1990s)
docs.text: Connected the world's computers, then (via the World Wide Web) the world's people. Collapsed the cost of communication to near zero and rewired society.

docs.title: GPS (1978 → 1990s)
docs.text: A constellation of satellites that tells any device exactly where it is. It quietly runs navigation, logistics, farming, banking timestamps, and disaster response.

docs.title: The smartphone (2007)
docs.text: Folded the camera, computer, internet, GPS, and telephone into one object — and put a supercomputer in ~4.5 billion pockets.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
Invention What it collapsed the cost of Printing press Copying knowledge Steam engine Physical power Electricity Light and motion, anywhere Computer Calculation Internet Communication Smartphone Access to all of the above

Innovator's lesson

Every world-changing invention dramatically lowered the cost of something fundamental. When you have an idea, ask: what does this make cheap that used to be expensive? See Innovations.

docs.title: Maths & Science
docs.text: The breakthroughs that changed how we see reality.

docs.title: The Mandelbrot set (pictured above)
docs.text: One of the simplest equations in mathematics — z → z² + c — produces a shape of literally infinite complexity. Zoom in forever and you never run out of new detail. It's the flagship of fractal geometry, which turned out to describe coastlines, lungs, blood vessels, and market crashes.

docs.title: Zero and infinity
docs.text: Invented in India (Brahmagupta, 7th century), the number zero is arguably the most important invention in mathematics — without it, no algebra, no calculus, no computers.

docs.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931)
docs.text: Kurt Gödel proved that in any consistent mathematical system, there are true statements that can never be proven. Mathematics proved its own limits — one of the most mind-bending results in human history.

docs.title: Euler's identity
docs.text: $\(e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0\)$ Five fundamental constants, one equation. Often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics.

docs.title: Relativity (Einstein, 1905 & 1915)
docs.text: Time runs slower when you move fast or sit deep in gravity. This isn't theory — your phone's GPS corrects for it every second, or maps would drift 10 km per day.

docs.title: Quantum mechanics
docs.text: At the smallest scales, particles exist in multiple states at once until measured, and can be entangled — linked so that measuring one instantly affects the other, across any distance. Einstein hated it ("spooky action at a distance"). Experiments keep proving it right.

docs.title: DNA (1953)
docs.text: Four letters — A, T, G, C — encode every living thing. We went from discovering the structure to editing it (CRISPR, 2012) in one human lifetime.

docs.title: Germ theory
docs.text:
Before the 1860s, doctors didn't wash their hands and surgery was a death sentence. The single idea that invisible organisms cause disease has saved more lives than any other discovery.

Pattern to notice

Every breakthrough above was resisted at first — Semmelweis was ridiculed for suggesting handwashing; Einstein's Nobel citation avoided mentioning relativity. Big ideas look wrong before they look obvious.

docs.title: Medical Science & The Human Body
docs.text: The most sophisticated machine we know is the one you're using to read this.

docs.title: The body by the numbers
docs.text:
• 37 trillion cells, each a tiny factory
  • 86 billion neurons in the brain, ~100 trillion connections
  • 100,000 km of blood vessels — 2.5 times around the Earth
  • Your heart beats ~100,000 times a day, ~3 billion times in a lifetime
  • You replace most of your cells every 7–10 years (see Ship of Theseus)

docs.title: Organs & systems
docs.text: Each organ is an engineering marvel: the liver performs 500+ chemical functions; the kidneys filter your entire blood volume ~40 times a day; the immune system remembers every pathogen it has ever met.

docs.title: Genetics
docs.text: Your DNA is a 3-billion-letter instruction manual, coiled into every cell. Since CRISPR (2012), we can edit it — the first CRISPR therapy (for sickle-cell disease) was approved in 2023, curing a genetic disease at its source.

docs.title: Medical breakthroughs that changed everything
docs.text:
• Anesthesia (1846) — made modern surgery possible
  • Antibiotics (1928) — turned fatal infections routine (now threatened, see antibiotic resistance)
  • Vaccines — eradicated smallpox, nearly polio
  • Organ transplants — first heart transplant 1967; now routine
  • mRNA platform — enabled COVID vaccines in months, now aimed at cancer

docs.title: Longevity & the future
docs.text: Human lifespan has roughly doubled in 150 years — mostly from clean water, vaccines, and antibiotics. The next frontier is healthspan: not just living longer, but staying healthy. See reverse aging.

docs.title: Regenerative medicine
docs.text:
Growing replacement tissue and organs from a patient's own cells — lab-grown bladders and windpipes already exist; 3D-bioprinted organs are in development. It could end transplant waiting lists.

Quote

Medicine is where "impossible" turns to "routine" fastest. A century ago, a scraped knee could kill you. The remaining giants — cancer, aging, dementia — are tracked in Unsolved: Medicine.

docs.title: Mind & Beyond
docs.text: Telepathy. Telekinesis. Teleportation. Psychology. The frontier between science fiction and laboratory fact — and it's moving faster than most people realize.

docs.title: Telepathy — mind to mind
docs.text:
The dream: transmitting thoughts directly between minds.

What's already real:

  • Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) — Neuralink, Synchron, and university labs have implanted chips that let paralyzed people type, move cursors, and control robotic arms by thought alone.
  • Brain-to-brain communication — in a 2014 experiment, a person in India sent the words "hola" and "ciao" to a person in France using only EEG (reading the brain) and TMS (writing to the brain). Crude, slow — but it happened.
  • Speech decoding — AI models in 2023–2025 reconstructed sentences a person was imagining from brain scans with growing accuracy.

Honest status: natural telepathy has never survived a controlled experiment. But technological telepathy is an engineering problem now, not a fantasy.

docs.title: Telekinesis — mind over matter
docs.text:
The dream: moving objects with the mind.

What's already real: thought-controlled prosthetic limbs, wheelchairs, drones, and robotic arms. A paralyzed person picking up a cup with a robot arm driven by their motor cortex is telekinesis — with wires as the missing link.

Honest status: no evidence minds can push matter directly. Every lab claim (spoon bending included) has collapsed under controlled conditions. The engineered version, though, is already changing lives.

docs.title: Teleportation — being there instantly
docs.text:
What's already real: quantum teleportation — the state of a particle has been transferred to another particle over 1,200 km (via satellite, China 2017). This is real, repeatable physics.

The honest catch: it transfers information, not matter, and the original state is destroyed in the process. Teleporting a human would mean scanning ~10²⁸ atoms — and philosophy kicks in hard: would the person arriving still be you? (See Philosophy — this is the Ship of Theseus problem.)

docs.title: Psychology — the operating system of the mind
docs.text:
The most practical frontier of all, because you use it every day:

  • Neuroplasticity — the brain rewires itself throughout life. Skills, habits, even recovery from injury are physical rewiring. You are always under construction.
  • Cognitive biases — 180+ documented ways the mind fools itself (confirmation bias, sunk cost, anchoring). Innovators who know their biases beat innovators who don't.
  • Flow state — deep focus where performance peaks and time vanishes. Triggered by clear goals + immediate feedback + challenge slightly above skill.
  • The placebo effect — belief alone produces measurable healing. The mind-body link isn't mystical; it's biochemical, and we're only starting to map it.

The Tekmaturix stance

Stay curious about everything, but demand evidence for anything. The real superpowers aren't paranormal — they're neuroplasticity, focus, and the courage (Matu 𒁍) to keep learning. And the engineered versions of telepathy and telekinesis are arriving within our lifetime.

docs.title: Earth's Natural Wonders
docs.text: The planet is the most spectacular engineer of all.

docs.title: Volcanoes
docs.text: Earth has ~1,500 potentially active volcanoes. They're destroyers and creators — they built the Hawaiian Islands, enriched the soil that feeds billions, and released the gases that formed our atmosphere and oceans. Supervolcanoes like Yellowstone could alter global climate.

docs.title: Earthquakes
docs.text: The planet's crust is broken into moving plates; where they grind, energy builds and releases. The largest ever recorded (Chile, 1960, magnitude 9.5) released more energy than thousands of nuclear bombs. Prediction remains unsolved.

docs.title: Mountains
docs.text: The Himalayas are still growing ~1 cm/year as India crashes into Asia. Everest's summit is marine limestone — once an ocean floor, now the roof of the world.

docs.title: Caves
docs.text: Sơn Đoòng in Vietnam is the largest cave passage on Earth — big enough to hold a 45-storey skyscraper, with its own jungle and clouds inside.

docs.title: Deserts
docs.text: The Sahara is as large as the United States and was green with lakes and hippos just 6,000 years ago — proof that Earth's climate swings dramatically over time.

docs.title: Forests
docs.text: The Amazon produces a huge share of the world's oxygen and holds ~10% of all known species. A single hectare can contain more tree species than all of North America.

docs.title: Rivers
docs.text: The Amazon River discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers combined — so much that it freshens the Atlantic Ocean 100 km offshore.

docs.title: Weather phenomena
docs.text:
From lightning (hotter than the Sun's surface) to hurricanes (releasing the energy of 10,000 nuclear bombs) to the auroras painted by solar wind — weather is the atmosphere's raw power made visible.

Tip

Understanding these forces isn't just wonder — it's survival. Predicting earthquakes, eruptions, and extreme weather are active Unsolved challenges.

docs.title: Oceans
docs.text: The frontier below us. We have better maps of Mars than of our own seafloor.

docs.title: The scale of the unknown
docs.text:
• Oceans cover 71% of Earth — yet more than 80% remains unmapped and unexplored.
  • More people have walked on the Moon (12) than have reached the deepest point of the ocean, Challenger Deep (fewer than 30 as of the mid-2020s).
  • Scientists estimate hundreds of thousands of marine species are still undiscovered.
  • The ocean produces over half the oxygen you breathe — thank phytoplankton, not just trees.

docs.title: Why the ocean matters for innovation
Medicine from the deep
docs.text: Ziconotide (a painkiller 1,000× more potent than morphine, non-addictive) comes from cone snail venom. Cancer drugs from sea sponges. Deep-sea organisms survive crushing pressure, no light, and near-freezing temperatures — their biochemistry is a library of solutions evolution already invented.

docs.title: Climate engine
docs.text: The ocean absorbs ~30% of human CO₂ and ~90% of excess heat. Understand the ocean, and you understand the climate's future.

docs.title: Energy and food
docs.text: Offshore wind, tidal power, wave energy, sustainable aquaculture — the ocean could power and feed billions without a single new oil well.

docs.title: The problems worth solving
docs.text:
• Plastic — 8 million tonnes enter the ocean yearly. Interception at rivers is the highest-leverage fix (10 rivers carry most of it).
  • Coral bleaching — reefs support 25% of marine life; heat-resistant coral breeding and reef restoration are active frontiers.
  • Deep-sea mapping — autonomous underwater drones are doing for the seafloor what satellites did for land. The Seabed 2030 project aims to map it all.

docs.title: More to explore
docs.text:
• Deep-sea creatures — anglerfish, giant squid, and bioluminescent life adapted to crushing pressure and total darkness. New species are found on nearly every deep dive.
  • Ocean mysteries — the "bloop" sounds, unexplained migrations, and whole ecosystems around hydrothermal vents that live on chemistry, not sunlight.
  • Underwater volcanoes — most of Earth's volcanic activity happens underwater, building islands and hosting life found nowhere else.
  • Shipwrecks — time capsules on the seafloor, from ancient trade ships to the Titanic, preserved in the cold and dark.
  • Marine technology — autonomous submarines, deep-sea drones, and sensors mapping a world we've barely seen.
  • Ocean conservation — protecting reefs, fisheries, and the carbon-absorbing systems that keep the whole planet livable.

The takeaway

Space gets the headlines, but the ocean is closer, cheaper to reach, and just as unexplored. For an innovator, it may be the most underrated frontier on (or off) Earth.

Open frontiers: mapping the seafloor, rogue-wave prediction, and global plastic cleanup are tracked in Unsolved: Oceans.

docs.title: Philosophy & Philanthropy
docs.text: Thinking well — and turning good thinking into good action.

docs.title: Who are you, really?
docs.text: The Ship of Theseus: if every plank of a ship is replaced over the years, is it still the same ship? Your body replaces most of its atoms every few years — so what makes you you? (This is also why teleportation is a philosophy problem, not just physics — see Mind & Beyond.)

docs.title: How do you know anything?
docs.text: Descartes doubted everything and found one bedrock: "I think, therefore I am." Science itself is philosophy applied — every experiment is an answer to the question "how would I know if I'm wrong?"

docs.title: What is a good life?
docs.text:
• Stoicism (Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus): control what you can, accept what you can't, and focus all energy on the first category. The ancient operating system that modern cognitive therapy is built on.
  • Aristotle: happiness isn't a feeling, it's eudaimonia — a life of practiced excellence. You become what you repeatedly do.

docs.title: Ideas worth wrestling with
docs.text:
• If an AI says it's conscious, how could we ever verify it?
  • Is mathematics invented or discovered?
  • Does free will exist if the brain is physics?

docs.title: Philanthropy — thinking that acts
docs.text:
Philosophy asks "what is good?" Philanthropy answers with action.

  • Effective altruism asks a simple, sharp question: for the same effort, how much good can I do? A $2 anti-malarial bed net can matter more than a $200 gesture.
  • Knowledge philanthropy — Wikipedia, free education (Khan Academy), open-source software prove that giving away knowledge multiplies it. This site is a small bet on the same idea.
  • The founder's pattern — Carnegie built 2,500 libraries; today's equivalent is funding vaccines, clean water, and open research. Wealth's highest use has always been leverage on human potential.

The connection

Tek gives you capability, Matu gives you persistence, but Rix — leadership — is measured by what you build for others. Innovation that helps no one is just decoration.

docs.title: Space
docs.text: The universe above us — and humanity's next frontier.

docs.title: Numbers that break the brain
docs.text:
• The observable universe holds roughly 2 trillion galaxies, each with hundreds of billions of stars.
  • Light from the Pillars of Creation (above) left 6,500 years ago — before the pyramids were built.
  • There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
  • Neutron stars are so dense that one teaspoon weighs about 4 billion tonnes.

docs.title: Reusable rockets
docs.text: Cost to orbit has fallen from ~\(65,000/kg (Space Shuttle) toward ~\)1,500/kg (Falcon 9) — and Starship aims for under $100/kg. Cheap access to orbit changes everything: manufacturing, energy, exploration.

docs.title: Exoplanets
docs.text: First confirmed in 1992. Today: 5,000+ known planets around other stars, dozens in habitable zones. The James Webb Space Telescope is now reading their atmospheres for biosignatures — we may detect alien life chemically before we ever hear a signal.

docs.title: Gravitational waves (2015)
docs.text: Colliding black holes ripple spacetime itself, and we built a machine (LIGO) sensitive enough to feel it — a measurement 10,000× smaller than a proton. A completely new sense organ for astronomy.

docs.title: The big open questions
docs.text:
• Dark matter & dark energy — 95% of the universe is made of something we cannot see and do not understand. The biggest unsolved problem in physics.
  • Are we alone? — the Fermi paradox: with 2 trillion galaxies, where is everybody?
  • Can humans become multiplanetary? — Mars settlement is now an engineering and biology problem (radiation, gravity, food), not a fantasy.

docs.title: More to explore
docs.text:
• Black holes — regions where gravity is so strong not even light escapes. We've now photographed two (M87 in 2019, our own galaxy's Sagittarius A* in 2022).
  • NASA & ESA missions — Artemis (back to the Moon), Europa Clipper (Jupiter's icy moon), and the ongoing Voyager probes, now in interstellar space after 45+ years.
  • James Webb discoveries — the most powerful telescope ever, seeing galaxies from the universe's first few hundred million years and sniffing exoplanet atmospheres.
  • Astronaut stories — from Gagarin's first orbit to a year aboard the ISS; the human side of the frontier.
  • Space technology — spinoffs from the space program touch daily life: memory foam, GPS, water filtration, camera sensors, cordless tools.

Quote

"The Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in a cradle forever." — Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, 1911

Open frontiers: the biggest space mysteries — dark matter, alien life, interstellar travel — are tracked in Unsolved: Space.

docs.title: Unsolved
docs.text:
A living map of what humanity still hasn't figured out.

Most websites document what we know. This section tracks what we don't — the biggest open problems in science, technology, and society. As breakthroughs happen, statuses change. That's the point: this page should look different every year.

docs.title: The progress tracker
docs.text:
Every problem gets a status:

Status Meaning 🔴 Unsolved No credible path to a solution yet 🟠 Early Research Serious work has begun, fundamentals still missing 🟡 Active Progress Real momentum — labs, funding, measurable advances 🟢 Mostly Solved Core problem cracked, deployment/scale remaining 🔵 Solved Done — moved to the history books

docs.title: 🤖 Unsolved: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text: Problem Status Difficulty Safe AGI 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AI alignment 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ AI consciousness — is it possible? 🔴 Unsolved ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Explainable AI 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Eliminating AI bias 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ AI governance 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Eliminating hallucinations 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ General-purpose robots 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Human-level reasoning 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: AI alignment
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #13

Why it matters — an AI system more capable than its builders must reliably want what humanity wants — even in situations nobody anticipated. Get this wrong at high capability levels and there may be no second attempt.

Current approaches — reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, interpretability research (reading a model's internal representations), scalable oversight (using AI to help supervise AI).

Major challenges — human values are inconsistent and hard to specify; models can learn to appear aligned; capabilities are advancing faster than alignment science.

Who is working on it — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, academic groups (MIRI, CHAI, Redwood Research), and national AI safety institutes.

Predicted timeline — must be solved before AGI arrives — which is exactly why it's urgent.

Related problems — safe AGI, AI governance, explainable AI.

docs.title: Safe Artificial General Intelligence
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #1

Why it matters — AGI could compress a century of scientific progress into a decade — curing diseases, solving fusion, understanding the brain. Built carelessly, it's also the technology with the highest stakes in human history.

Current approaches — scaling laws research, frontier-model safety testing, red-teaming, international coordination (AI safety summits since 2023).

Major challenges — nobody agrees on what AGI is, when it arrives, or how to test safety for capabilities that don't exist yet. Competitive pressure rewards speed over caution.

Predicted timeline — expert estimates range from a few years to many decades — the disagreement is itself part of the problem.

docs.title: AI consciousness
docs.text:
Status: 🔴 Unsolved · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — if an AI could suffer or have experiences, everything about how we build and use it changes morally.

Major challenges — we can't even verify consciousness in each other except by analogy — see the hard problem of consciousness. There is no agreed test that distinguishes "reports being conscious" from "is conscious."

Related problems — what is consciousness?, digital minds ethics.

docs.text: Problem Status Difficulty What is consciousness? 🔴 Unsolved ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Can lost memories be restored? 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Cure Alzheimer's disease 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Cure Parkinson's disease 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Why do we dream? 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ High-bandwidth brain-computer interfaces 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Reading thoughts safely & ethically 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Intelligence enhancement 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Complete human brain map (connectome) 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Mechanisms of mental illness 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: What is consciousness?
docs.text:
Status: 🔴 Unsolved · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — it's the deepest question there is: why does information processing feel like something from the inside? It decides how we treat animals, patients in comas, and possibly AI.

Current approaches — Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, and adversarial experiments designed to make the theories fight (a landmark head-to-head study reported in 2023 wounded both).

Major challenges — the "hard problem": even a complete wiring diagram of the brain wouldn't obviously explain why experience exists at all.

Predicted timeline — no consensus even on whether it's solvable.

Related problems — AI consciousness, anesthesia mechanisms, the nature of dreams.

docs.title: Cure Alzheimer's disease
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #7

Why it matters — 55+ million people live with dementia; numbers will triple by 2050 as populations age. It erases the person before it takes the body.

Current approaches — anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab — the first drugs to slow the disease, approved 2023–2024), blood-based early diagnostics, tau- targeting drugs, and prevention via cardiovascular health.

Major challenges — by the time symptoms appear, the brain has been under attack for 20 years. The amyloid hypothesis explains some cases, not all.

Latest breakthrough — blood tests that detect Alzheimer's pathology years before symptoms (rolling out mid-2020s) — early treatment is the real unlock.

Predicted timeline — meaningful slowing: now. Prevention: 2030s. Reversal: unknown.

docs.title: Complete human brain map
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — 86 billion neurons, ~100 trillion connections. Mapping them is to neuroscience what the genome was to biology.

Latest breakthrough — the complete fruit-fly connectome (140,000 neurons) was finished in 2024; a full mouse brain is the next milestone. A cubic millimeter of human cortex was mapped in 2024 — it took 1.4 petabytes.

Major challenges — a whole human brain at that resolution would require more storage than currently exists on Earth. New compression and imaging tech required.

Related problems — brain-computer interfaces, mental illness mechanisms.

docs.title: Practical quantum computers
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #12

Why it matters — quantum computers could crack problems classical machines never will: designing drugs and materials atom-by-atom, modeling chemistry exactly, and optimizing impossibly complex systems.

Current approaches — superconducting qubits (IBM, Google), trapped ions (Quantinuum), photonics, and neutral atoms — no clear winner yet. Error correction is the central race.

Major challenges — qubits are fragile; they lose their quantum state (decoherence) in microseconds and errors accumulate fast. Useful computation needs thousands of stable logical qubits built from millions of physical ones.

Latest breakthrough — Google's 2024 "Willow" chip showed error rates that fall as the system scales — a key signal that fault tolerance is reachable.

Predicted timeline — useful, error-corrected machines: early-to-mid 2030s for narrow problems.

Related problems — fault-tolerant systems, post-quantum security, quantum internet.

docs.title: Post-quantum cybersecurity
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — a large quantum computer would break the encryption protecting almost all of today's internet, banking, and secrets. Adversaries may be harvesting encrypted data now to decrypt later.

Current approaches — new "quantum-resistant" algorithms — the US NIST standardized the first set in 2024, and a global migration is beginning.

Major challenges — replacing encryption across every device, protocol, and system on Earth is a decade-long project that must finish before quantum computers mature.

docs.title: Quantum internet
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — a network using quantum entanglement would be unhackable by the laws of physics, and would link quantum computers together.

Latest breakthrough — entanglement distributed over metropolitan-scale fiber networks and via satellite (China's Micius); small multi-node quantum networks now exist.

Major challenges — entanglement is fragile over distance; quantum repeaters (the equivalent of signal boosters) are still immature.

docs.title: Commercial fusion energy
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #2

Why it matters — fusion is the power source of the stars: near-limitless energy from seawater, no long-lived radioactive waste, no carbon. It would rewrite geopolitics and climate at once.

Current approaches — magnetic confinement (ITER, the giant international tokamak; private firms like Commonwealth Fusion using high-temperature superconductors), inertial confinement (lasers — the US National Ignition Facility), and dozens of startups with novel designs.

Major challenges — sustaining a plasma hotter than the Sun's core, getting more energy out than in continuously (not just for an instant), and doing it economically.

Latest breakthrough — the National Ignition Facility achieved net energy gain from a fusion reaction in December 2022, and repeated it — a historic physics milestone (though the whole facility still consumed far more power than the reaction released).

Predicted timeline — pilot plants in the 2030s; grid-scale commercial fusion 2040s if milestones hold. "Always 30 years away" is finally shrinking.

docs.title: Affordable desalination
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — the ocean holds 97% of Earth's water; making it drinkable cheaply would end water scarcity for coastal billions.

Current approaches — reverse osmosis (mature but energy-hungry), next-gen graphene and biomimetic membranes, and pairing plants with solar/renewable power.

Major challenges — energy cost and brine disposal (concentrated salt harms marine life). Inland regions can't easily use it.

Related problems — universal clean water, ocean farming.

docs.title: Carbon removal at scale
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #9

Why it matters — cutting emissions isn't enough; to hit climate targets we must also pull CO₂ back out of the air — billions of tonnes per year.

Current approaches — direct air capture (giant fans + chemistry), enhanced rock weathering, reforestation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, biochar.

Major challenges — current direct air capture costs hundreds of dollars per tonne and captures thousands of tonnes — we need billions of tonnes at a fraction of the cost.

Predicted timeline — meaningful scale requires 2030s–2040s cost breakthroughs.

docs.title: Space elevator
docs.text:
Status: 🔴 Unsolved · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — a cable from the ground to geostationary orbit would let cargo ride to space for a tiny fraction of rocket cost — the single biggest possible change to space access.

Current approaches — mostly theoretical. Research into ultra-strong tethers (carbon nanotubes, graphene, and boron nitride); some propose a lunar elevator first, which is feasible with existing materials.

Major challenges — no manufactured material is remotely strong-enough-yet-light- enough for an Earth cable ~36,000 km long. Space debris and weather add more.

Predicted timeline — Earth version: not this generation. Lunar version: plausibly mid-century.

Related problems — self-healing materials, asteroid mining.

docs.title: Battery breakthroughs
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — batteries are the bottleneck for electric cars, grid storage of renewables, and portable everything. Better batteries unlock the whole clean-energy transition.

Current approaches — solid-state batteries (safer, denser — Toyota and QuantumScape racing to production), sodium-ion (cheap, no scarce lithium), lithium-sulfur, and grid-scale flow batteries.

Major challenges — the trade-off triangle of energy density vs. cost vs. safety vs. lifespan — improving one usually hurts another.

Latest breakthrough — solid-state cells hit lab milestones (2023–2025); first commercial vehicles expected late 2020s.

docs.title: Self-healing materials
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — infrastructure that repairs its own cracks would slash maintenance costs and prevent catastrophic failures in bridges, pipes, and planes.

Latest breakthrough — self-healing concrete (bacteria that precipitate limestone to seal cracks) and self-healing polymers are in early real-world deployment.

docs.title: Lunar cities
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — the Moon is a 3-day trip away, a proving ground for Mars, and a source of water ice (fuel) and rare materials. A permanent base is the realistic first step to humanity living off-Earth.

Current approaches — NASA's Artemis program (crewed return this decade), planned lunar gateway station, and research into building with lunar regolith (3D-printed habitats using local dust) to avoid shipping everything from Earth.

Major challenges — lunar dust is razor-sharp and clings to everything; 14-day nights need stored power; radiation with no atmosphere; and the sheer cost.

Predicted timeline — small research base 2030s; a real "city" is a multi-decade goal.

Related problems — Mars settlement, space manufacturing, asteroid mining.

docs.title: Synthetic biology
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — engineering biology like software lets us program cells to make medicines, food, fuels, and materials — even organisms that never existed in nature.

Current approaches — engineered microbes producing insulin, spider silk, and fragrances; a synthetic minimal cell (JCVI-syn3.0) built with just 473 genes; DNA as data storage.

Major challenges — biology is messy and unpredictable; engineered organisms behave differently outside the lab. Serious biosafety and biosecurity concerns.

Related problems — organ regeneration, reverse aging.

docs.title: Digital consciousness / mind uploading
docs.text:
Status: 🔴 Unsolved · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — copying a mind into a computer would redefine death, identity, and what it means to be human.

Major challenges — we can't yet map a single human brain (see The Brain), we don't understand consciousness, and even a perfect copy raises the Ship of Theseus question: would the upload be you, or a copy that merely thinks it is?

Predicted timeline — deeply speculative; not this century on current science.

docs.title: Cure all cancers
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — cancer is not one disease but hundreds, and it touches nearly every family.

Current approaches — immunotherapy (training the immune system — CAR-T cells have cured some previously terminal blood cancers), mRNA cancer vaccines (personalized, in trials), early detection via blood tests (liquid biopsy), targeted therapies.

Major challenges — cancer evolves and resists treatment; solid tumors hide from the immune system; what cures one cancer often does nothing for another.

Latest breakthrough — personalized mRNA vaccines showed strong results against melanoma and pancreatic cancer in trials (2023–2024).

Predicted timeline — "cure" is the wrong frame — cancer is becoming a managed disease, cancer by cancer, over the coming decades.

docs.title: Reverse aging
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #6

Why it matters — aging is the single biggest risk factor for cancer, dementia, and heart disease. Slow it, and you delay all of them at once.

Current approaches — cellular reprogramming (partial Yamanaka factors rejuvenated cells and even restored sight in mice), senolytics (clearing "zombie" cells), targeting the hallmarks of aging.

Major challenges — reprogramming too far turns cells cancerous; human trials are slow because the endpoint (living longer) takes decades to measure.

Predicted timeline — healthspan extension: plausibly 2030s–2040s. Dramatic lifespan extension: speculative.

Related problems — organ regeneration, longevity beyond 120 (Future Humanity).

docs.title: Eliminate antibiotic resistance
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — resistant bacteria could kill 10 million people/year by 2050, making routine surgery and chemotherapy dangerous again. A slow-motion pandemic.

Current approaches — new antibiotic classes (AI-discovered candidates like halicin), bacteriophage therapy (viruses that eat bacteria), and stewardship to slow resistance.

Major challenges — antibiotics are unprofitable (used briefly, then shelved), so the pipeline is nearly empty. Evolution always eventually wins.

Latest breakthrough — machine learning discovered structurally novel antibiotics (2023–2024) after decades with almost no new classes.

docs.text: Problem Status Difficulty Mapping the entire ocean floor 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐ Global-scale ocean plastic cleanup 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Predicting rogue waves 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐ Complete deep-sea biodiversity catalog 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Sustainable ocean farming at scale 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐ Coral reef restoration 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Ocean carbon removal 🟠 Early Research ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Reliable tsunami prediction 🟡 Active Progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Underwater habitats / cities 🔴 Unsolved ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: Mapping the entire ocean floor
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #10

Why it matters — we can't protect, understand, or use what we haven't seen. Seafloor shape drives tsunamis, currents, climate, and hides most of Earth's biology.

Current approaches — the Seabed 2030 project coordinates ships and autonomous underwater drones worldwide; satellite altimetry fills gaps at low resolution.

Major challenges — the ocean is opaque to radar; mapping requires physically sending sound waves from ships or drones over 360 million km². Slow and expensive.

Latest breakthrough — coverage rose from ~6% (2017) to ~25%+ (mid-2020s) — genuine acceleration, driven by autonomous vessels.

Predicted timeline — 2030s for a complete first-pass map if funding holds.

docs.title: Global-scale ocean plastic cleanup
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — 8M tonnes/year enter the ocean; microplastics are now in rain, food, and human blood.

Current approaches — river interception (10 rivers carry a large share of the inflow — the cheapest leverage point), The Ocean Cleanup's gyre systems, plastic-eating enzymes (PETase), and material substitution upstream.

Major challenges — microplastics are effectively unrecoverable once dispersed; cleanup must beat the inflow rate or it's bailing a leaking boat.

Predicted timeline — river interception can scale this decade; open-ocean legacy plastic is a 50+ year problem.

Related problems — plastic alternatives, sustainable packaging.

docs.title: Predicting rogue waves
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — walls of water 20–30 m high appear without warning and have sunk ships that were built to survive "any" storm. Long dismissed as sailors' myth — until one was measured directly (Draupner platform, 1995).

Current approaches — AI models trained on wave-buoy data can now flag conditions that breed rogue waves minutes to hours ahead.

Major challenges — the waves emerge from nonlinear interactions that amplify chaotically — tiny measurement errors destroy forecasts.

Latest breakthrough — machine-learning models (2023–2025) predict rogue-wave likelihood significantly better than physics-only models.

docs.title: End extreme poverty
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · Grand Challenge #14

Why it matters — extreme poverty is the root cause behind hunger, preventable disease, and lost human potential at massive scale.

Current approaches — the share of humanity in extreme poverty fell from ~40% (1980) to under 10% today — one of history's great underreported successes. Tools: economic growth, direct cash transfers (proven highly effective), mobile banking, and targeted global health programs.

Major challenges — the remaining poverty is concentrated in conflict zones and fragile states where growth and aid are hardest to deliver. Climate change threatens to reverse gains.

Predicted timeline — near-elimination is achievable by ~2050 if conflict and climate don't undo progress.

Related problems — food security, universal education.

docs.title: Universal quality education
docs.text:
Status: 🟡 Active Progress · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — education is the highest-leverage investment in human potential; it compounds across generations.

Current approaches — free online learning (Khan Academy, open courseware), AI tutors that personalize instruction, low-cost devices, and mobile-first content for regions without classrooms.

Major challenges — access is necessary but not sufficient — quality, teacher support, and motivation matter more than content availability. Connectivity gaps persist.

Latest development — AI tutors (2023 onward) show promise as personalized, always-available teachers — a possible step-change for underserved learners.

docs.title: Housing affordability
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — housing is the largest cost in most people's lives; unaffordable housing drives inequality, homelessness, and declining birth rates.

Current approaches — modular/prefab construction, 3D-printed homes, zoning reform to allow density, and mass timber for faster cheaper mid-rise buildings.

Major challenges — the problem is as much political (land use, regulation) as technical. Construction productivity has barely improved in 50 years.

docs.title: What is dark matter?
docs.text:
Status: 🔴 Unsolved · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — galaxies spin too fast to hold together with the gravity of visible matter alone. Something invisible makes up ~27% of the universe, and we have no idea what it is.

Current approaches — underground detectors (LUX-ZEPLIN, XENONnT) hunting for particles; the Large Hadron Collider; telescopes mapping gravitational lensing.

Major challenges — decades of increasingly sensitive detectors have found nothing. Either the particle is stranger than theorized, or our theory of gravity itself is wrong.

Latest breakthrough — the Euclid space telescope (launched 2023) is building the largest 3D dark-matter map ever made.

Predicted timeline — genuinely unknown. Could be next year, could be a century.

Related problems — dark energy, quantum gravity.

docs.title: Are we alone in the universe?
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — either answer changes everything about how humanity sees itself.

Current approaches — James Webb reading exoplanet atmospheres for biosignatures; Mars sample return; missions to icy moons (Europa Clipper, arriving 2030); SETI scanning for signals.

Major challenges — a single microbe would settle it, but life may be rare, hidden under ice, or chemically unfamiliar. Absence of evidence is hard to interpret (the Fermi paradox).

Latest breakthrough — JWST has detected carbon-based molecules in exoplanet atmospheres; possible biosignature candidates remain contested.

Predicted timeline — microbial evidence plausible within 10–30 years; intelligent life — unknowable.

docs.title: Sustainable Mars colonization
docs.text:
Status: 🟠 Early Research · Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Why it matters — a second home makes civilization resilient to planetary disasters.

Current approaches — SpaceX Starship (mass cargo to Mars), NASA Artemis (Moon first as proving ground), ISRU experiments (MOXIE made oxygen from Martian air in 2021).

Major challenges — radiation, 38% gravity's effect on the human body over years, growing food, closed-loop life support, and the psychology of isolation.

Predicted timeline — first crewed landing possibly 2030s; a self-sustaining settlement is a 50–100 year project.

Related problems — artificial gravity, closed-loop agriculture.

docs.title: Problem Profile Template
docs.text:
Copy this structure for every new problem added to the Unsolved section:

### Problem Name

**Status:** 🟡 Active Progress · **Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ · **Category:** Space

**Why it matters** — one or two sentences on the stakes.

**Current approaches** — the main strategies being tried.

**Major challenges** — why it isn't solved yet.

**Who is working on it** — labs, companies, countries.

**Latest breakthrough** — most recent significant progress (with year).

**Predicted timeline** — honest estimate, ranges are fine.

**Related problems** — links to connected challenges.

docs.title: Status levels
docs.text:
• 🔴 Unsolved — no credible path yet
  • 🟠 Early Research — fundamentals still missing
  • 🟡 Active Progress — real momentum
  • 🟢 Mostly Solved — deployment remaining
  • 🔵 Solved — done

docs.title: Rules for this section
docs.text:
1. Be honest about status — no hype. If a company claims fusion "in 5 years," the status is still what the physics says.
  2. Update, don't rewrite — when progress happens, change the status and add the breakthrough. The edit history is the story.
  3. Cite the real players — name actual labs and missions so readers can follow up.
